section.title: Learning the foundations pays off even when you stop using the syntax
section.deck: David Malan explains why CS50 uses C before moving to higher-level tools.

blocks.question: Why begin with C when teaching programming?
answer: Malan sees C as a useful teaching balance: it is close enough to hardware to reveal how programs work, but has more approachable syntax than assembly or machine code. Loops, conditions, functions, variables, and return values make it possible to introduce procedural programming through a relatively small language.

Its limited standard-library support creates a deliberate learning opportunity. Students build data structures rather than immediately instantiate them from a library. In CS50, that includes hash tables, linked lists, trees, tries, stacks, and queues. The purpose is not to make everyone write those implementations repeatedly throughout a career. It is to understand the representations and algorithms underneath the convenient interface.

That understanding has three benefits in his account: better choices when designing data structures, the ability to diagnose failures from first principles, and a foundation for using higher-level languages intelligently. Moving from a substantial C hash-table implementation to a Python dictionary in one line makes the abstraction visible. Malan acknowledges that Python-first teaching can be productive and that CS50 has used it for some audiences; the C-first route serves the course’s broader goals of engineering understanding and technological literacy.
blocks.speaker: David Malan

blocks.question: What would you say to someone who argues that a future web engineer does not need these low-level topics?
answer: Malan rejects the conclusion that knowledge is useless because the corresponding language will not be used every day. He distinguishes knowing the underlying principles from literally using a particular implementation tool. Someone describing themselves as a full-stack engineer, in his view, should understand the layers in that stack.

He uses his own teaching as an example: he works in C during a limited part of the course, and Scratch during an even shorter part, while using other languages more frequently. The earlier material still helps him reason about performance, system behavior, and the design of a new solution. His standard for engineering is therefore understanding and creating beyond simply producing code. It is an educational argument, not a requirement that every engineer use C for every task.
